## Questions so far?

\center

![](../questions.jpg){width=40%}

## Diversity as a community property

A JSDM produces a lot of output: intercepts, slopes, associations, predicted probabilities for every species at every site. Rich, but hard to communicate.

\pause

Diversity indices — species richness, Shannon entropy, Simpson's index — are scalar summaries of the community matrix $\mathbf{Y}$.

\pause

\textbf{If we model the community, diversity follows.}

## Why model-based diversity?

Indices such as Shannon entropy and Simpson's index have no generative model: there is no likelihood, no data-generating process, nothing to fit or check.

\pause

Without a generative model:

\begin{itemize}
  \item No uncertainty quantification: no standard errors, no confidence intervals
  \item No ability to account for sampling: effort, detection probability, protocol differences
  \item No ability to account for data properties: overdispersion, zero-inflation, censoring
  \item No prediction for new sites, times, or conditions
\end{itemize}

\pause

A community model addresses all of these: diversity follows from the generative model and inherits its inferential properties.

# Species richness

## What is species richness?

Species richness $SR_i$ at site $i$ is the number of species recorded:

\begin{equation}
SR_i = \sum_{j=1}^{m} y_{ij} \quad \text{(for binary data)}
\end{equation}

\pause

It is by far the most common biodiversity metric: simple to calculate, intuitive to interpret, and widely used in conservation and ecology.

\pause

But it is a \textbf{derived quantity} from multivariate community data. Analyzing it directly means throwing away most of the data.

## The typical approach

Species richness is most commonly analyzed with Poisson or negative-binomial regression:

\begin{equation}
\log\{\mathbb{E}(SR_i)\} = \alpha + \textbf{x}_i^\top \symbf{\beta}
\end{equation}

\pause

This is simple and interpretable. But it rests on four assumptions that are routinely violated in practice:

1. Species are \textbf{independent} of each other
2. All species respond \textbf{identically} to the environment
3. The species pool is \textbf{infinite} (unbounded distribution)
4. The Poisson or NB distribution is \textbf{appropriate}

## Assumption 1: species independence

Species are not independent; they share environmental responses and co-occur non-randomly. \newline

\pause

If species co-occurrence is positive, species richness has \textbf{less} variance than a Poisson.
If it is negative, species richness has \textbf{more} variance.

\pause

A Poisson or NB regression cannot accommodate this: it will over- or underestimate uncertainty.

## Assumption 2: homogeneity of niches

A Poisson or NB distribution for species richness is only justified if all species respond the same way to the environment, i.e., have the same niche.

\pause

This is ecologically unrealistic: species have different distributions, different ranges, different optimums.

\pause

The consequence: estimated coefficients from a Poisson richness regression are a \textbf{weighted average} over species, with weights depending on the distribution of species' niches, usually not the average ecologists want.

## Assumption 3: an infinite species pool

A Poisson distribution is unbounded above: it can predict species richness larger than the number of species in your data.

\pause

\textbf{This is ecologically impossible.} You cannot observe more species than those you have observed. \newline

Negative-binomial adds overdispersion, making the problem worse. \newline

\pause

Species richness is inherently bounded by the number of species in the observed pool.

## The correct distribution: Poisson-Binomial

Under species independence and Bernoulli responses, species richness follows a \textbf{Poisson-Binomial distribution}:

\begin{equation}
SR_i \sim \mathcal{PB}(\pi_{i1}, \pi_{i2}, \ldots, \pi_{im})
\end{equation}

with

\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}(SR_i) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \pi_{ij}, \qquad \text{var}(SR_i) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \pi_{ij}(1-\pi_{ij})
\end{equation}

\pause

- Mean richness = \textbf{sum of species' occurrence probabilities}
- Variance is bounded (cannot exceed $m/4$)
- This is the distribution that actually generates species richness
- The Binomial is a special case (all $\pi_{ij}$ equal)

## Why univariate analysis fails

\columnsbegin
\column{0.5\textwidth}

```{r pb_vs_pois, echo=FALSE, fig.height=8, message=FALSE}
set.seed(42)
m <- 30
pi_j <- rbeta(m, 2, 5)
pb_mean <- sum(pi_j)
pb_var <- sum(pi_j*(1-pi_j))

k <- 0:m
# Poisson-Binomial via simulation
pb_sim <- replicate(10000, sum(rbinom(m, 1, pi_j)))
pois_pmf <- dpois(k, pb_mean)

par(mar=c(4,4,2,1))
hist(pb_sim, breaks=seq(-0.5, m+0.5, 1), freq=FALSE,
     col="steelblue", border="white",
     xlab="Species richness", ylab="Probability",
     main="Poisson-Binomial vs. Poisson", cex.main = 2.5, cex.lab = 2.5)
lines(k, pois_pmf, col="firebrick", lwd=3, type="b", pch=16)
legend("topright", legend=c("True (Poisson-Binomial)","Poisson approximation"),
       fill=c("steelblue", NA), lty=c(NA,1), col=c(NA,"firebrick"),
       pch=c(NA,16), border=c("steelblue",NA), bty="n", cex = 2)
```

\column{0.5\textwidth}

The Poisson distribution:

- Puts probability mass on impossible values (SR > m)
- Has the wrong shape (underdispersed here)
- Assumes the wrong mean-variance relationship

The mismatch worsens when species niches are heterogeneous.

\columnsend

## Species richness as an emergent property

We do not model species richness directly; instead, \textbf{species richness emerges} from each species' response to the environment:

\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}(SR_i) = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \mathbb{E}\{I(y_{ij} > 0)\} = \sum_{j=1}^{m} p(y_{ij} > 0)
\end{equation}

\pause

- No separate richness model needed
- Works for any data type: binary, counts, cover, biomass, ordinal
- Uncertainty propagates naturally from species-level predictions
- Assumptions are explicit and testable
- Non-linear richness gradients emerge even from linear species responses

## Works for any data type

For any distribution with zero support, the probability of presence can be derived:

\footnotesize

\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Data type & Distribution & $p(y_{ij} > 0)$ \\
\midrule
Binary   & Bernoulli        & $\pi_{ij}$ \\
Count    & Poisson          & $1 - e^{-\mu_{ij}}$ \\
Count    & Negative-binomial & $1 - (1 + \mu_{ij}/k)^{-k}$ \\
Biomass  & Tweedie          & $1 - \text{Tw}(0;\, \mu_{ij}, \phi_j, p)$ \\
Cover    & Ordered beta     & $1 - \rho_{ij}^0$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\normalsize

\pause

The only requirement: the distribution must assign probability mass at zero. Gamma and beta distributions do not.

## Implementation in gllvm

The `predictSR()` function computes:

- Expected species richness $\hat{S}_i = \sum_j \hat{p}_{ij}$
- Full Poisson-Binomial distribution at each site
- Prediction intervals; optionally for new predictor values
- Per-species AUC via `goodnessOfFit()`: well-calibrated $\hat{p}_{ij}$ give well-calibrated $\hat{S}_i$

```{r, eval=FALSE}
sr_pred <- predictSR(model, newX = newdata,
                     newLV = matrix(0, ncol = 2, nrow = nrow(newX)))
sr_pred$expected     # expected species richness
residuals(sr_pred, model)   # Dunn-Smyth residuals
goodnessOfFit(Y, object = model, measure = "AUC") # AUC per species
```

# Example 1

## Example: alpine plants in Switzerland

```{r alpine_dat, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
Y <- read.csv("../data/alpineY.csv")[,-1]
X <- read.csv("../data/alpineX.csv")[,-1]
X <- X[rowSums(Y) > 0, ]
Y <- Y[rowSums(Y) > 0, ]
X_scaled <- data.frame(scale(X[, sapply(X, is.numeric)]))
```

- Data by [D'Amen et al. (2018)](https://nsojournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/ecog.03148)
- Occurrence of 175 species at 840 plots
- Binary data (presence-absence)
- Sampled on an elevation gradient in Switzerland

```{r}
dim(Y)
```

## Example: fit a JSDM

\footnotesize

```{r jsdm_fit, cache=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, echo = -1}
TMB::openmp(parallel::detectCores(),autopar=TRUE, DLL = "gllvm")
model <- gllvm(y = Y[,c(59,(1:ncol(Y))[-59])], X = X_scaled,
               formula = ~ELEV,
               num.lv = 2,
               family = "binomial",
               sd.errors = FALSE)
```

We include elevation as a fixed covariate and two latent variables to capture residual species associations.

## Example: a Poisson GLM for species richness

```{r glm_lin_plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.5, message=FALSE, cache=TRUE, dependson="alpine_dat"}
obs_sr      <- rowSums(Y)
glm_lin     <- glm(obs_sr ~ ELEV, data = X_scaled, family = poisson)
elev_ord    <- order(X_scaled$ELEV)
elev_sorted <- X_scaled$ELEV[elev_ord]
pois_pred   <- predict(glm_lin, newdata = data.frame(ELEV = elev_sorted), type = "response")

par(mar=c(4,4,1,1))
plot(X_scaled$ELEV, obs_sr, pch=16, col=rgb(0,0,0,0.3),
     xlab="Elevation (scaled)", ylab="Species richness", main=NA)
lines(elev_sorted, pois_pred, col="steelblue", lwd=2)
legend("topright", legend=c("Observed", "Poisson GLM (linear ELEV)"),
       pch=c(16,NA), lty=c(NA,1),
       col=c(rgb(0,0,0,0.3),"steelblue"), bty="n")
```

A Poisson GLM with linear elevation predicts a monotone richness curve. Does the multispecies model agree?

## Example: LV-elevation confounding

\footnotesize

```{r sr_confound, cache=FALSE, message=FALSE}
obs_sr  <- rowSums(Y)
sr_full <- predictSR(model, se.fit = FALSE)
sr_marg <- predictSR(model, se.fit = FALSE, newLV = matrix(0, ncol = 2, nrow = nrow(Y)))
```

```{r sr_confound_plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.2, message=FALSE}
par(mar=c(4,4,1,1))
plot(X_scaled$ELEV, obs_sr, pch=16, col=rgb(0,0,0,0.3),
     xlab="Elevation (scaled)", ylab="Species richness", main=NA)
points(X_scaled$ELEV, sr_full$expected$fit, pch=16, col=rgb(0.7,0,0,0.5))
points(X_scaled$ELEV, sr_marg$expected$fit, pch=16, col=rgb(0,0,0.8,0.4))
legend("topright", legend=c("Observed", "Full model", "Marginal (LV = 0)"),
       pch=16, col=c(rgb(0,0,0,0.3), rgb(0.7,0,0,0.5), rgb(0,0,0.8,0.4)), bty="n")
```

## Example: SR residuals, linear elevation term

```{r sr_resid_linear, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4.5, message=FALSE, cache=FALSE}
res_marg <- residuals(sr_marg, model)
res_full <- residuals(sr_full, model)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
plot(res_marg$fitted, res_marg$residuals,
     xlab = "", xaxt = "n", ylab = "Dunn-Smyth residuals", main = "Marginal")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(res_marg$residuals, main = "QQ (marginal)", xlab = "", xaxt = "n", ylab = "", yaxt = "n")
qqline(res_marg$residuals)
plot(X_scaled$ELEV, res_marg$residuals,
     xlab = "", xaxt = "n", ylab = "", yaxt = "n", main = "Marginal vs. elevation")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
plot(res_full$fitted, res_full$residuals,
     xlab = "Expected SR", ylab = "Dunn-Smyth residuals", main = "Conditional")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(res_full$residuals, main = "QQ (conditional)", ylab = "", yaxt = "n")
qqline(res_full$residuals)
plot(X_scaled$ELEV, res_full$residuals,
     xlab = "Elevation (scaled)", ylab = "", yaxt = "n", main = "Conditional vs. elevation")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
```

Marginal residuals (LV = 0) reveal the arch the linear fixed effect misses; conditional residuals are flat because the latent variables absorb the curvature.

## Example: adding a quadratic term

\footnotesize

```{r jsdm_fit2, cache=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
model_lin <- model
model <- gllvm(y = Y[,c(59,(1:ncol(Y))[-59])], X = X_scaled,
               formula = ~ELEV + I(ELEV^2),
               num.lv = 2,
               family = "binomial",
               sd.errors = TRUE)
```

Species richness peaks at intermediate elevation. Without $\text{ELEV}^2$ in the fixed effects, the latent variables absorb the curvature and new-site predictions fail. Adding the quadratic keeps the nonlinearity in the fixed effects where it belongs.

## Example: why plot(model) does not reveal this

\begin{itemize}
  \item \texttt{plot(model)} uses \textbf{conditional} fitted values: latent variables are estimated per site and adapt to each model
  \item A missing quadratic term is absorbed by the latent variables; conditional residuals look clean for both models
  \item Marginal predictions (LV $= 0$) reveal the discrepancy
\end{itemize}

```{r species_plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.5, message=FALSE, cache=TRUE, dependson="jsdm_fit2"}
elev_seq  <- seq(min(X_scaled$ELEV), max(X_scaled$ELEV), length.out = 100)
newX_pred <- data.frame(ELEV = elev_seq)
newLV_0   <- matrix(0, ncol = 2, nrow = 100)

pred_lin  <- predict(model_lin, newX = newX_pred, newLV = newLV_0, type = "response")
pred_quad <- predict(model,     newX = newX_pred, newLV = newLV_0, type = "response")

amp <- apply(pred_quad, 2, function(x) diff(range(x)))
spp <- order(amp, decreasing = TRUE)[1:2]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (k in seq_along(spp)) {
  j <- spp[k]
  plot(X_scaled$ELEV, jitter(Y[, j], amount = 0.03), pch = 3,
       col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.15), ylim = c(-0.05, 1.05),
       xlab = "Elevation (scaled)", ylab = "Occurrence probability",
       main = colnames(Y)[j])
  lines(elev_seq, pred_lin[, j],  col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
  lines(elev_seq, pred_quad[, j], col = "firebrick",  lwd = 2)
  if (k == 1L) {
    legend("topleft", legend = c("Observed", "Linear ELEV", "ELEV + ELEV^2"),
           pch = c(3, NA, NA), lty = c(NA, 1, 1),
           col = c(rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.3), "steelblue", "firebrick"), bty = "n")
  }
}
```

## Example: comparing predictions

```{r sr_plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4, message=FALSE, cache=TRUE, dependson="jsdm_fit2"}
elev_seq <- seq(min(X_scaled$ELEV), max(X_scaled$ELEV), length.out = 100)
newX     <- data.frame(ELEV = elev_seq)
srnew    <- predictSR(model, newX = newX, se.fit = 200,
                      newLV = matrix(0, ncol = model$num.lv, nrow = nrow(newX)))
glm_pois  <- glm(obs_sr ~ ELEV + I(ELEV^2), data = X_scaled, family = poisson)
pois_pred <- predict(glm_pois, newdata = newX, type = "link",  se.fit = TRUE)

par(mar=c(4,4,1,1))
plot(X_scaled$ELEV, obs_sr, pch=16, col=rgb(0,0,0,0.3),
     xlab="Elevation (scaled)", ylab="Species richness",
     main=NA, ylim=c(0, max(max(exp(pois_pred$fit)), max(obs_sr),
                            max(srnew$expected$upper, na.rm=TRUE)) + 5))
polygon(c(elev_seq, rev(elev_seq)),
        c(srnew$expected$lower, rev(srnew$expected$upper)),
        col=adjustcolor("firebrick", alpha.f=0.3), border=NA)
abline(h = ncol(Y), lty=3, col="gray50")
lines(elev_seq, srnew$expected$fit, col="firebrick", lwd=3)
lines(elev_seq, exp(pois_pred$fit), col="steelblue", lwd=3)
UI = exp(pois_pred$fit+pois_pred$se.fit*qnorm(0.975))
LI = exp(pois_pred$fit+pois_pred$se.fit*qnorm(1-0.975))
polygon(c(elev_seq, rev(elev_seq)),
        c(LI, rev(UI)),
        col=adjustcolor("steelblue", alpha.f = 0.3), border=NA)
legend("topright", legend=c("Observed", "Multispecies model (95% CI)", "Poisson GLM (95% CI)"),
       pch=c(16,NA,NA), lty=c(NA,1,1),
       col=c(rgb(0,0,0),"firebrick","steelblue"), bty="n")
```

\textbf{Question:} Both models include a quadratic elevation term. Why do their predictions differ?

## Example: residual diagnostics

```{r sr_resid, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.5, message=FALSE}
sr  <- predictSR(model, se.fit = FALSE)
res <- residuals(sr, model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(res$fitted, res$residuals, xlab = "Expected SR", ylab = "Dunn-Smyth residuals")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(res$residuals); qqline(res$residuals)
plot(X_scaled$ELEV, res$residuals, xlab = "Elevation (scaled)", ylab = "Dunn-Smyth residuals")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
```

Poisson-Binomial quantile residuals: no systematic elevation trend remains after adding the quadratic term.

# Diversity

## From richness to diversity

Species richness is one dimension of diversity — and the model gives us a tractable distribution for it.

\pause

But diversity has many facets: how dominant is the community at a site? How similar are nearby sites? How variable is composition across the region?

\pause

These all follow from the \textbf{variance structure of $\eta_{ij}$} — like $R^2$ in mixed models \footnotesize (Nakagawa \& Schielzeth 2013)\normalsize, we work on the link scale rather than the response scale.

## Alpha, beta, and gamma diversity

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Alpha}: local diversity at a single site; how uneven is the community here?
  \item \textbf{Gamma}: regional diversity; how much variation is there across the whole community?
  \item \textbf{Beta}: turnover between sites; how different are two communities?
\end{itemize}

\pause

In a model, these follow from the \textbf{variance-covariance structure} of $\eta_{ij}$

\pause

\textcolor{red}{The following slides present calculations for a specific model. Results are model-dependent.}

## Dominance

For $\eta_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + \mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{\beta}_j$ with $\beta_{0j} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2_{\beta_0})$ and $\mathbf{\beta}_j \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\Sigma_\beta)$:

\begin{equation}
D_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top\Sigma_\beta\mathbf{x}_i
\end{equation}

\pause

\begin{itemize}
  \item Large $D_i$: strong environmental filtering; a few well-adapted species dominate
  \item Small $D_i$: weak environmental sorting; more even composition
\end{itemize}

## Gamma diversity

Gamma diversity is the expected within-site variation over sites:

\begin{equation}
\gamma = \sigma^2_{\beta_0} + \mathbb{E}_i(D_i)
\end{equation}

\pause

Regional diversity decomposes into a baseline $\sigma^2_{\beta_0}$ (species differ even at the environmental centroid) and average dominance $\mathbb{E}_i(D_i)$ (the contribution of environmental sorting across sites).

## Pairwise similarity (beta diversity)

Pairwise similarity between sites $i$ and $k$ is the covariance of the linear predictor across species:

\begin{equation}
\text{cov}_j(\eta_{ij}, \eta_{kj}) = \sigma^2_{\beta_0} + \mathbf{x}_i^\top\Sigma_\beta\mathbf{x}_k
\end{equation}

\pause

\begin{itemize}
  \item $\sigma^2_{\beta_0}$: baseline similarity shared by all site pairs
  \item $\mathbf{x}_i^\top\Sigma_\beta\mathbf{x}_k$: environmental similarity; large when sites share the same environment
\end{itemize}

## Turnover

Turnover between sites $i$ and $k$ follows from the covariance structure:

\begin{align}
\text{var}_j(\eta_{ij} - \eta_{kj}) &= \text{var}_j(\eta_{ij}) + \text{var}_j(\eta_{kj}) - 2\,\text{cov}_j(\eta_{ij},\eta_{kj}) \notag \\
&= \sigma^2_{\beta_0} + D_i + \sigma^2_{\beta_0} + D_k - 2\left(\sigma^2_{\beta_0} + \mathbf{x}_i^\top\Sigma_\beta\mathbf{x}_k\right) \notag \\
&= (\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_k)^\top\Sigma_\beta(\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_k)
\end{align}

\pause

The baseline $\sigma^2_{\beta_0}$ cancels. Turnover has the same quadratic form as $D_i$, evaluated at the difference $\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_k$.

## Uniqueness

The average pairwise similarity of site $i$ with all other sites is:

\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}_k\!\left\{\text{cov}_j(\eta_{ij},\eta_{kj})\right\} = \sigma^2_{\beta_0} + \mathbf{x}_i^\top\Sigma_\beta\bar{\mathbf{x}}
\end{equation}

\pause

\textbf{Uniqueness} is the average dissimilarity of site $i$ from all other sites:

\begin{equation}
\text{uniqueness}_i = \mathbb{E}_k\!\left\{\text{var}_j(\eta_{ij}-\eta_{kj})\right\} = \sigma^2_{\beta_0} + D_i + \gamma - 2\left(\sigma^2_{\beta_0} + \mathbf{x}_i^\top\Sigma_\beta\bar{\mathbf{x}}\right)
\end{equation}

\pause

Sites at environmental extremes have high uniqueness: their communities differ most from the regional average — potential refugia, range edges, endemic communities.

# Example 2

## Example: Swiss birds

Swiss breeding bird atlas: 56 species at 1000+ sites, with temperature (bio\_1), precipitation (bio\_12), and slope.

\pause

Fit a JSDM with random species-specific slopes, no LVs:

\footnotesize
```{r birds_show, eval=FALSE}
model_birds <- gllvm(Y, X, formula = ~(bio_1 + bio_12 + slp | 1),
                     family = "binomial", num.lv = 0, beta0com = TRUE)
```
\normalsize

\pause

$\hat{\Sigma}_\beta$ is then the estimated covariance of random slopes. All diversity quantities follow from it.

## Predicting dominance

```{r maprep, echo = FALSE, cache = TRUE, cache.lazy = FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
avi_dat <- read.csv('../data/SwissBirds.csv')
y_birds <- as.matrix(avi_dat[,1:56])
X_birds <- avi_dat[,-c(1:56)]
X_birds <- X_birds[rowSums(y_birds)>0, ]
y_birds <- y_birds[rowSums(y_birds)>0,]
X_birds <- X_birds[,-which(apply(X_birds,2,anyNA))]
X_birds <- data.frame(sapply(X_birds,function(x)if(is.numeric(x)){scale(x)}else{x}, simplify = FALSE))
model_birds <- gllvm(y_birds, X = X_birds, formula = ~(bio_1+bio_12+slp|1),
                     family = "binomial", num.lv = 0, beta0com = TRUE)
model_birds_lv <- gllvm(y_birds, X = X_birds, formula = ~(bio_1+bio_12+slp|1),
                        family = "binomial", num.lv = 2, beta0com = TRUE)
bio1_scale  <- scale(avi_dat$bio_1)
bio12_scale <- scale(avi_dat$bio_12)
slp_scale   <- scale(avi_dat$slp)
source("../1Tuesday/switzerland/slope.R")
bio <- geodata::worldclim_country("CHE", var = "bio", res = 0.5, path = tempdir())
bio_1_proj  <- project(bio[[1]],  crs(slope)); ext(bio_1_proj)  <- ext(slope)
bio_12_proj <- project(bio[[12]], crs(slope)); ext(bio_12_proj) <- ext(slope)
bio_1_rast  <- resample(bio_1_proj,  slope)
bio_12_rast <- resample(bio_12_proj, slope)
x <- as.matrix(data.frame(
    1,
    (values(bio_1_rast)  - attr(bio1_scale,  "scaled:center")) / attr(bio1_scale,  "scaled:scale"),
    (values(bio_12_rast) - attr(bio12_scale, "scaled:center")) / attr(bio12_scale, "scaled:scale"),
    (values(slope)       - attr(slp_scale,   "scaled:center")) / attr(slp_scale,   "scaled:scale")))
alpha <- slope
terra::values(alpha) <- rowSums(x * (x %*% model_birds$params$sigmaB))
# Site-level quantities (training data)
SigB       <- model_birds$params$sigmaB
x_sites    <- as.matrix(cbind(1, X_birds[, c("bio_1", "bio_12", "slp")]))
D_sites      <- rowSums(x_sites * (x_sites %*% SigB))
gamma_val    <- mean(D_sites)
sigma2_alpha <- SigB[1L, 1L]
x_bar        <- colMeans(x_sites)
uniqueness   <- D_sites + gamma_val - 2*as.numeric(x_sites %*% SigB %*% x_bar)
D_grid           <- rowSums(x * (x %*% SigB))
uniqueness_rast  <- alpha
terra::values(uniqueness_rast) <- D_grid + gamma_val - 2 * as.numeric(x %*% SigB %*% x_bar)
```

```{r pairwise, echo=FALSE, cache=TRUE, cache.lazy=FALSE, dependson="maprep"}
set.seed(42)
samp       <- sample(nrow(x_sites), min(80L, nrow(x_sites)))
pairs      <- combn(samp, 2L)
env_sim    <- apply(pairs, 2L, function(p)
  as.numeric(x_sites[p[1L], ] %*% SigB %*% x_sites[p[2L], ]))
env_turn   <- apply(pairs, 2L, function(p) {
  dx <- x_sites[p[1L], ] - x_sites[p[2L], ]
  as.numeric(dx %*% SigB %*% dx)
})
delta_bio1 <- apply(pairs, 2L, function(p)
  abs(X_birds$bio_1[p[1L]] - X_birds$bio_1[p[2L]]))
SigLambda  <- crossprod(model_birds_lv$params$theta) / ncol(y_birds)
lv_u       <- model_birds_lv$lvs[samp, , drop = FALSE]
lv_turn    <- apply(pairs, 2L, function(p) {
  i <- match(p[1L], samp); k <- match(p[2L], samp)
  du <- lv_u[i, ] - lv_u[k, ]
  as.numeric(du %*% SigLambda %*% du)
})
```

\footnotesize
```{r dom_calc, eval=FALSE}
terra::values(alpha) <- rowSums(x * (x %*% model_birds$params$sigmaB))
```
\normalsize

`model_birds$params$sigmaB` is $\hat{\Sigma}_\beta$: the estimated covariance matrix of random slopes. This evaluates $D_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top\hat{\Sigma}_\beta\mathbf{x}_i$ at each grid cell: the environmental component of alpha diversity (dominance) due to temperature, precipitation, and slope.

## Dominance of Swiss birds

```{r map, dpi = 300, echo = FALSE, cache = TRUE, dependson="maprep", warning=FALSE,message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
dat <- as.data.frame(alpha,xy=TRUE) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(x, y), names_to = "layer", values_to = "value")

plt<-ggplot() +
  theme_classic()+theme(axis.text=element_blank(), axis.ticks=element_blank())+scale_fill_viridis_c(name="Dominance", na.value="white")+geom_raster(data=dat, aes(x=x, y=y, fill = value), interpolate=TRUE)+coord_fixed()+xlab(NULL)+ylab(NULL)+ggtitle("Bird dominance (due to temperature, precipitation and slope)")
plt
```

## Extending to LVs

Adding $\mathbf{u}_i^\top\mathbf{\lambda}_j$ to the linear predictor introduces residual species associations not captured by environment. Each diversity quantity gains an extra term:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Within-site variation}: $\sigma^2_{\beta_0} + D_i + \mathbf{u}_i^\top\!\tfrac{1}{m}\Lambda^\top\!\Lambda\,\mathbf{u}_i$
  \item \textbf{Turnover}: $\Delta\mathbf{x}^\top\Sigma_\beta\Delta\mathbf{x} + \Delta\mathbf{u}^\top\!\tfrac{1}{m}\Lambda^\top\!\Lambda\,\Delta\mathbf{u}$
  \item \textbf{Avg.\ pairwise similarity}: $\sigma^2_{\beta_0} + \mathbf{x}_i^\top\Sigma_\beta\bar{\mathbf{x}}$, unchanged (LV scores are centered, $\bar{\mathbf{u}} \approx \mathbf{0}$)
\end{itemize}

\pause

LVs primarily inflate uniqueness (through alpha) and add residual turnover. Gamma and uniqueness extend analogously.

## Example: pairwise similarity

```{r sim_plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.5, message=FALSE, cache=TRUE, dependson="pairwise"}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(delta_bio1, env_sim,
     pch = 16, col = rgb(0.1, 0.4, 0.7, 0.3),
     xlab = expression("|" * Delta * "bio_1|  (temperature difference, scaled)"),
     ylab = "Pairwise similarity",
     main = NA)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
```

Pairwise similarity decreases with temperature difference. Pairs at opposite ends of the gradient can be negative: their species compositions are anti-correlated, not merely dissimilar.

## Example: pairwise turnover

```{r turnover_plot, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.5, message=FALSE, cache=TRUE, dependson="pairwise"}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(delta_bio1, env_turn + lv_turn,
     pch = 16, col = rgb(0.5, 0, 0.5, 0.3),
     xlab = expression("|" * Delta * "bio_1|  (temperature difference, scaled)"),
     ylab = "Pairwise turnover",
     main = NA)
points(delta_bio1, env_turn,
       pch = 16, col = rgb(0.1, 0.4, 0.7, 0.3))
legend("topleft",
       legend = c(expression(Delta * bold(x)^T * Sigma[beta] * Delta * bold(x) ~ "(env. only)"),
                  expression(+ ~ Delta * bold(u)^T * Sigma[Lambda] * Delta * bold(u) ~ "(+ LV)")),
       pch = 16, col = c(rgb(0.1, 0.4, 0.7, 0.6), rgb(0.5, 0, 0.5, 0.6)), bty = "n")
```

Environmental turnover increases with temperature difference; the LV component adds residual community dissimilarity not explained by the measured predictors. Averaging pairwise turnover over all partners $k$ gives uniqueness: the per-site expected departure from the rest of the landscape.

## Example: uniqueness

```{r uniqueness_plot, echo=FALSE, dpi=300, cache=TRUE, dependson="maprep", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
dat_u <- as.data.frame(uniqueness_rast, xy = TRUE) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -c(x, y), names_to = "layer", values_to = "value")
ggplot() +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank()) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Uniqueness", na.value = "white") +
  geom_raster(data = dat_u, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = value), interpolate = TRUE) +
  coord_fixed() + xlab(NULL) + ylab(NULL) +
  ggtitle("Bird uniqueness (environmental distance from regional average)")
```

Sites at environmental extremes are the most unique: their communities differ most from the regional average. These are the sites that drive beta diversity.

# Summary

## Summary

- Model the community; diversity follows
- Univariate species richness analyses make strong and routinely violated assumptions
- Variance components connect to alpha, beta, and gamma diversity; $D_i$ captures environmental dominance
- Uniqueness quantifies how much a site's community differs from the regional average

\pause

\centering

\textbf{Modelling species richness well requires modelling species well first.}
